quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the five count systems, what each measures and which fibres use it.

questions.q: An indirect count system measures:
questions.explain: Indirect systems such as Ne and Nm count length (hanks or metres) per unit weight, so the number rises as the yarn gets finer. Weight per unit length is the direct family.

questions.q: English cotton count Ne is defined as the number of:
questions.explain: Ne counts 840-yd hanks per lb. 560 yd is the worsted hank, and the metric system uses metres per gram, not hanks.

questions.q: Tex is the weight in grams of:
questions.explain: Tex is grams per 1,000 m. Grams per 9,000 m is denier and grams per 10,000 m is decitex.

questions.q: Which count system is the ISO universal one?
questions.explain: Tex is the universal ISO system; Ne is used for cotton, Nm for wool and worsted in Europe, and denier for silk and filament.

questions.q: In a direct system a finer yarn has a lower number.
questions.explain: Direct systems record weight per unit length; a finer yarn weighs less per 1,000 m (or 9,000 m), so its tex or denier is lower.

questions.q: Denier is traditionally used for which yarns?
questions.explain: Denier (grams per 9,000 m) is the filament system used for silk, synthetic filament and Lycra; cotton uses Ne and worsted uses Nm.

questions.q: Metric count Nm equals:
questions.explain: Nm is metres per gram, which is the same as kilometres per kilogram. Metres per kilogram would be 1,000 times larger.

questions.q: Decitex and grex are two names for the same unit.
questions.explain: The lecture lists decitex, dtex (grex) as grams per 10,000 m; grex is the older name for the same measure.

questions.q: Which two systems are indirect?
questions.explain: Ne (hanks per pound) and Nm (metres per gram) are indirect; tex, dtex and denier are all direct.

questions.q: The converter on the page works every conversion through one intermediate system. Which?
questions.explain: Each known count is first turned into tex, and Ne, denier, Nm and dtex are then derived from tex with the four fixed relations.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The constant 590.67 and the four relations that tie Ne, tex, denier, dtex and Nm together.

questions.q: Which relation links Ne and tex?
questions.explain: Because Ne is indirect and tex direct, their product is constant: Ne × tex = 590.67. Multiplying tex by Ne instead of dividing is a common slip.

questions.q: Denier is obtained from tex by:
questions.explain: Denier is grams per 9,000 m, nine times the length of tex, so denier = 9 × tex. 10 × tex is dtex and 1,000 ÷ tex is Nm.

questions.q: Metric count Nm is obtained from tex by:
questions.explain: Tex is g per 1,000 m and Nm is m per g, so Nm = 1,000 ÷ tex. 590.67 ÷ tex gives Ne, not Nm.

questions.q: If the Ne of a yarn doubles, its tex:
questions.explain: Ne × tex is constant, so doubling Ne halves tex; the yarn is twice as fine and weighs half as much per 1,000 m.

questions.q: The constant 590.67 comes from 453.6 g per pound divided by 768.1 m per hank, scaled to 1,000 m.
Which conversion of Ne to denier is correct?
questions.explain: Tex = 590.67 ÷ Ne and denier = 9 × tex, so denier = 5,316 ÷ Ne; 1 Ne is 5,316 denier. Multiplying by Ne reverses the direction.

questions.q: Two yarns: A is Ne 20 and B is Ne 40. Which is true?
options: A is finer and has lower tex
B is finer and has lower tex
B is coarser and has higher tex
questions.explain: Higher Ne means finer; Ne 40 is about 14.8 tex while Ne 20 is about 29.5 tex. Finer yarn, lower tex.

questions.q: dtex and denier of the same yarn are related by:
questions.explain: dtex = 10 × tex and denier = 9 × tex, so dtex = denier × 10 ÷ 9 — dtex is always slightly larger than denier (e.g. 150 denier = 166.7 dtex).

questions.q: Converting Nm to Ne needs a constant different from 590.67.
questions.explain: Go through tex: tex = 1,000 ÷ Nm, then Ne = 590.67 ÷ tex. Combining the two, Ne = Nm × 0.5907, which still rests on 590.67.

questions.q: The original worksheet divided by 1,458 (a denier figure) when converting to Ne. Why did it still work for the first row?
options: Because the first row happened to be 162 tex = 1,458 denier, so the division gave the right Ne by coincidence
Because denier and tex are equal for coarse yarns
Because Ne is a direct system
questions.explain: The first worked example is 162 tex, whose denier is 1,458; dividing by that cell matched only for that row. The correct constant is 590.67 on tex (or 5,316 on denier).

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Convert between the systems using Ne × tex = 590.67, denier = 9 × tex, dtex = 10 × tex and Nm = 1,000 ÷ tex.

questions.q: Convert Ne 40 to tex. Answer to two decimal places.
A yarn is 30 tex. What is its Ne, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: Ne = 590.67 ÷ tex = 590.67 ÷ 30 = 19.69 Ne — the rule of thumb Ne 20 ≈ 30 tex.

questions.q: What is the denier of a 20 tex yarn?
questions.explain: denier = 9 × tex = 9 × 20 = 180 denier.

questions.q: A filament yarn is 300 denier. Give its tex to two decimal places.
questions.explain: tex = denier ÷ 9 = 300 ÷ 9 = 33.33 tex.

questions.q: Convert Nm 40 to tex.
What is the metric count Nm of an Ne 20 yarn, to two decimal places?
Express 75 denier in dtex, to two decimal places.
A 40-denier Lycra yarn: what is its tex, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: tex = 40 ÷ 9 = 4.44 tex, about one-seventh of an Ne 20 yarn (29.5 tex).

questions.q: A 162 tex yarn is converted to Ne. Which answer is right?
questions.explain: Ne = 590.67 ÷ 162 = 3.65. Ne 27.4 would come from 162 ÷ 590.67 × 100, a reversed division; 1.62 and 16.2 are just decimal shifts.

questions.q: 150 denier converted to Nm gives:
questions.explain: tex = 150 ÷ 9 = 16.67; Nm = 1,000 ÷ 16.67 = 60. 16.67 is the tex and 35.44 the Ne of the same yarn; 1,350 is 150 × 9, a reversed step.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Supplier quotes, buyer specifications and mill situations where picking the right count system matters.

questions.q: A European buyer specifies a wool weft as Nm 48. Which system should you expect and what does the number mean?
questions.explain: Nm is the metric count used for wool and worsted in Europe: 48 metres per gram (48 km per kg).

questions.q: A supplier quotes polyester filament as 150/48. Which part is the count and in what system?
options: 150 is the denier of the yarn
48 is the denier of the yarn
150 is the Ne of the yarn
150 is the tex of the yarn
questions.explain: Filament yarns are quoted in denier; 150 denier with 48 filaments. 150 denier is 16.67 tex or about Ne 35.4.

questions.q: Your costing sheet works in Ne but a purchase order says 29.5 tex cotton. What should you enter?
questions.explain: Ne = 590.67 ÷ 29.5 ≈ 20. Entering 29.5 as if it were Ne would make the yarn seem much finer than it is.

questions.q: A merchandiser says a yarn of 40 denier is coarser than one of 40 tex because the systems are the same. How do you correct him?
options: He is right; denier and tex are interchangeable
40 denier is 4.44 tex, so it is far finer than 40 tex
40 denier is 360 tex, so it is far coarser
Denier cannot be compared with tex
questions.explain: tex = denier ÷ 9, so 40 denier = 4.44 tex, about nine times finer than 40 tex. Both are direct systems and compare easily once in the same unit.

questions.q: A mill can compare yarns from different suppliers only if all counts are first converted to one system.
questions.explain: Ne, Nm, tex and denier run in different directions and scales, so a fair comparison of fineness or price per weight needs one common system, usually tex.

questions.q: A knitting customer wants the same fineness as your Ne 30 cotton, but in the tex he uses. What do you quote?
questions.explain: 590.67 ÷ 30 = 19.69 tex. 50.8 is the Nm and 177 the denier of the same yarn.

questions.q: You are checking a count-conversion spreadsheet and find one row divides by a cell containing 1,458. What should you do?
options: Leave it: the row gives the right answer
Replace it with the constant 590.67 (for tex) so every row converts correctly
questions.explain: The lecture notes that dividing by the denier 1,458 only happened to work for the first row; the general constant for tex to Ne is 590.67.

questions.q: Core-spun denim yarn uses 70-denier Lycra inside Ne 10 cotton. Roughly how much finer is the Lycra than the cotton?
questions.explain: Ne 10 = 59.07 tex; 70 denier = 7.78 tex; 59.07 ÷ 7.78 ≈ 7.6, so the Lycra is about seven to eight times finer.

questions.q: A blend-yarn supplier (Europe) quotes Nm 34 and a local spinner quotes Ne 20 for the same purpose. Which is finer?
options: They are practically the same fineness
questions.explain: Nm 34 = 1,000 ÷ 34 = 29.4 tex; Ne 20 = 590.67 ÷ 20 = 29.5 tex. The two yarns are effectively the same count.

questions.q: A buyer's spec reads 'warp 30s, weft 20s'. In a Pakistani cotton mill what system is implied?
questions.explain: Cotton yarns in Pakistan are quoted in Ne; '30s' is Ne 30. The s simply marks the count number.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step conversions, common slips and the reasoning behind the constant — check your direction every time.

questions.q: Derive the denier of a 1 Ne yarn from 590.67 tex. Answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.explain: 1 Ne = 590.67 tex; denier = 9 × 590.67 = 5,316 denier.

questions.q: What is the Nm of a 1 Ne yarn, to three decimal places?
A student converts Ne 30 to tex and gets 0.0508. What did he do?
questions.explain: 30 ÷ 590.67 = 0.0508; the correct form is tex = 590.67 ÷ Ne = 19.69. The product Ne × tex must come to 590.67.

questions.q: A 2/30 Ne two-ply yarn is equivalent to Ne 15 single. What is its tex, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: The resultant count of two Ne 30 singles plied is Ne 15; tex = 590.67 ÷ 15 = 39.38 tex, twice the 19.69 tex of one single.

questions.q: A yarn is quoted as 1,620 dtex. Its Ne is about:
questions.explain: tex = 1,620 ÷ 10 = 162; Ne = 590.67 ÷ 162 = 3.65 — the first worked example in the lecture.

questions.q: Because denier = 9 × tex, an Ne 20 yarn of about 29.5 tex is about 266 denier.
questions.explain: 29.5 × 9 = 266 denier, matching the lecture's rule of thumb Ne 20 ≈ 30 tex ≈ 266 denier.

questions.q: Convert Nm 25 to Ne, to two decimal places.
questions.explain: tex = 1,000 ÷ 25 = 40; Ne = 590.67 ÷ 40 = 14.77 Ne, as in the lecture's last worked example.

questions.q: Which list is in order from finest to coarsest?
questions.explain: In tex: 40 denier = 4.4, Ne 40 = 14.8, Ne 20 = 29.5, 162 tex = 162. Lower tex is finer, so the order is 40 denier, Ne 40, Ne 20, 162 tex.

questions.q: If 1 lb were taken as 454 g and a hank as 768 m, the constant would be:
questions.explain: 454 × 1,000 ÷ 768 = 591.1; rounding the inputs shifts the constant a little. The lecture's 453.6 g and 768.1 m give 590.67.

questions.q: A 1,000-m length of yarn weighs 11.8 g. What is its Ne, to one decimal place?
